title: Apple pickers: a competitive labor market and one orchard, and a rise in the demand for apples
scenario: In the invented Tamsin Valley, many orchards sell apples in a perfectly competitive market and hire apple pickers in a perfectly competitive labor market. Brindle Orchard is one typical orchard. Assume the orchards maximize profit.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw correctly labeled side-by-side graphs for the labor market for apple pickers and for Brindle Orchard. On your graphs, show the market wage, labeled WM; the labor supply curve Brindle faces; and the number of pickers Brindle hires, labeled qF.

slips.MRP: MRP is the orchard's demand for pickers. The supply it faces is a horizontal line at the market wage.

rubric.point: Correctly labeled side-by-side graphs: Wage and Quantity of labor on both pairs of axes; DL and SL in the market; MRP for the orchard
accept: W and L (or Q of labor) on both graphs
D and S in the market, MRP or D = MRP for the firm

rubric.point: The orchard's labor supply is a horizontal line at WM, the wage where DL meets SL in the market, carried across from the market graph
accept: a horizontal line labeled S = MFC = W, MRC = W, or similar, at the market wage

rubric.point: qF is shown where the MRP curve meets the horizontal wage line (MRP = MFC)
accept: a dashed line from the MRP and wage-line crossing down to the quantity axis, labeled qF

parts.sample: Left graph (labor market): Wage on the vertical axis, Quantity of labor on the horizontal axis, a downward-sloping DL and an upward-sloping SL crossing at WM and QM, marked with dashed lines to both axes. Right graph (Brindle Orchard): Wage on the vertical axis, Quantity of labor on the horizontal axis, a horizontal line at WM labeled S = MFC = W, with a dashed line carrying WM across from the market graph, and a downward-sloping MRP curve. Brindle hires qF, where MRP crosses S = MFC = W, marked with a dashed line down to the quantity axis.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain why the labor supply curve that Brindle Orchard faces is horizontal.

rubric.point: Brindle hires so small a share of the pickers that it can hire as many as it wants at the market wage without changing it (it is a wage taker), so each extra picker costs exactly WM
accept: the orchard is a wage taker
each picker adds the same wage to cost, so MFC = W

parts.sample: Brindle is one of many orchards hiring pickers, so it is a wage taker: it can hire as many pickers as it wants at the market wage WM without changing that wage. Each additional picker therefore adds exactly WM to its costs, so the supply of labor it faces (and its MFC) is horizontal at WM.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Brindle Orchard's fifth picker adds 30 bushels of apples a day, and apples sell for \$4 a bushel. Calculate the marginal revenue product of the fifth picker. Show your work.

rubric.point: \$120 a day, with work shown: MRP = MP × P = 30 × \$4

parts.sample: Because Brindle sells apples in a perfectly competitive market, its marginal revenue is the price. MRP = MP × MR = 30 bushels × \$4 = \$120 a day.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The market wage for pickers is \$100 a day. (i) Identify whether Brindle Orchard will hire the fifth picker. (ii) Explain your answer using marginal analysis.

rubric.point: Yes, Brindle hires the fifth picker
Because the fifth picker's MRP (\$120) is greater than her MRC, the \$100 wage, so hiring her adds \$20 to profit (hire while MRP is at least MRC)

parts.sample: (i) Yes, Brindle hires the fifth picker. (ii) A profit-maximizing firm hires a worker if her marginal revenue product is at least her marginal resource cost. The fifth picker adds \$120 to revenue (MRP) and \$100 to cost (MRC = the wage), so hiring her raises profit by \$20.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The demand for apples increases. On a correctly labeled graph of the labor market for apple pickers, show the effect on the market wage and the number of pickers hired.

key.because: a rise in the demand for apples, which raises pickers' MRP

slips.SL: The demand for apples changes what pickers are worth to orchards, so the demand for pickers shifts; pickers' willingness to work is unchanged.

rubric.point: The labor demand curve shifts to the right (DL1 to DL2)
accept: a rightward shift of DL with an arrow

rubric.point: The new equilibrium shows a higher wage and a larger quantity of pickers (W2 above W1, Q2 to the right of Q1)
accept: the wage and the quantity of labor both rise, marked on the axes

parts.sample: In the labor market graph, DL shifts right from DL1 to DL2. The new crossing with SL is at a higher wage, W2, and a larger quantity of pickers, Q2, both marked with dashed lines to the axes.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Explain why the increase in the demand for apples changes the demand for apple pickers.

rubric.point: Every link of the chain: higher demand for apples raises the price of apples, which raises each picker's MRP (MP × P), so orchards want more pickers at each wage and labor demand increases
accept: the demand for pickers is derived from the demand for apples, through a higher apple price and a higher MRP

parts.sample: The demand for pickers is derived from the demand for apples. When the demand for apples increases, the market price of apples rises. Each picker's marginal revenue product, MP × P, rises with the price, so at every wage orchards want to hire more pickers: the demand for labor shifts to the right.
